content: Red eye in children is a frequent reason for medical consultations. While it is often a benign condition, it can sometimes lead to visual impairment. There are three types of red eye presentations: localized, diffuse, and perilimbal (perikeratic) injection. The perilimbal type is particularly important to identify, as it is associated with serious ocular diseases. Accurate diagnosis and prompt treatment are essential to avoid disrupting a child’s visual development. However, physical examination in children can be challenging. Referral to an ophthalmologist is warranted if there is diagnostic uncertainty, chronic pathology, or resistance to initial treatment. Viral and bacterial conjunctivitis are the most common causes and are generally self-limiting, with serious complications being rare. Red eye in children can be classified into three subtypes: localized, diffuse, and perikeratic injection. Microscopic histopathological analysis often reveals viral or bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, or Staphylococcus aureus. Fungal infections may also be observed. Common causes of red eye in children include blepharitis, cellulitis, conjunctivitis (pink eye), corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, eye allergies, fungal keratitis, glaucoma, herpes keratitis, pinguecula, pterygium, retinoblastoma, subconjunctival hemorrhage, and uveitis. Life-threatening causes, though rare, include conditions that can result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours if untreated. Red eye can occur in patients of all ages, but it is more commonly observed in males than females. There is no racial predisposition. Risk factors include upper respiratory infections, viral conjunctivitis, irritant conjunctivitis (e.g., exposure to smog or chlorinated pools), and bacterial conjunctivitis. Early clinical features of red eye include tearing, discharge, itching, pain, foreign body sensation, photophobia, and vision changes. Complications may include severe pain, visual loss, or corneal involvement, particularly in cases involving contact lens use, trauma, chemical injury, or recent eye surgery. Unilateral redness should raise suspicion for more serious conditions. Patients with red-flag symptoms or signs require immediate referral to an ophthalmologist. Prognosis is generally excellent, with most cases resolving within days unless associated with systemic illnesses. Diagnosis of red eye in children relies on a detailed patient history and thorough eye examination. Diagnostic criteria include reduced visual acuity, ciliary flush (circumcorneal injection), corneal abnormalities (e.g., edema or opacities), corneal staining, abnormal pupil size, and abnormal intraocular pressure. Symptoms may include eye discharge, pain, photophobia, itching, visual changes, and redness. Physical examination findings may include eyelid redness or swelling, periorbital cellulitis, acute ethmoiditis, corneal ulcers, herpes simplex keratitis, foreign bodies, blurred vision, or uveitis. Laboratory findings are generally nonspecific for red eye in children. However, elevated serum CRP or WBC levels may indicate bacterial conjunctivitis. Systemic symptoms may suggest an underlying systemic illness, such as rheumatic arthritis. Imaging studies like X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs are not routinely associated with red eye but may be useful in cases of trauma or complications. For example, CT scans are preferred for orbital injuries or intraocular foreign body localization, while MRIs may help diagnose complications of traumatic red eye. Ocular ultrasound is an indispensable tool for diagnosing and triaging ophthalmic emergencies. Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Recognizing the need for emergent referral to an ophthalmologist is critical in primary care management. Referral is necessary for severe pain unrelieved by topical anesthetics, vision loss, copious purulent discharge, corneal involvement, traumatic eye injury, recent ocular surgery, distorted pupils, herpes infection, or recurrent infections. Urgent ophthalmic consultation is required for chemical burns, intraocular infections, globe ruptures, perforations, and acute glaucoma. Medical therapy for red eye in children emphasizes good hygiene, such as frequent handwashing, to reduce the spread of viral conjunctivitis. Topical cyclosporine, corticosteroids, and systemic omega-3 fatty acids may be used for moderate dry eye. Chronic blepharitis unresponsive to eyelid hygiene and topical antibiotics may benefit from oral tetracycline or doxycycline. If the cornea is involved, intensive antibiotic eye drops and systemic antibiotics may be required. Surgical intervention is reserved for emergency cases, such as intraocular infections, globe ruptures, perforations, acute glaucoma, or traumatic eye injuries. Prevention involves practicing good hygiene to control the spread of red eye. Recommendations include avoiding touching the eyes, frequent handwashing, using clean towels, not sharing personal items, and replacing eye cosmetics regularly. Red eye is no more contagious than the common cold, and individuals can return to work, school, or childcare if they maintain proper hygiene. In newborns, red eye prevention is critical due to their susceptibility to bacteria in the birth canal, which can cause ophthalmia neonatorum, a severe form of conjunctivitis requiring immediate treatment to preserve vision. After birth, all newborns should have their eyes cleaned and receive antibiotic ointment, such as tetracycline, to prevent infection. Pregnant women with vaginal infections should be treated during antenatal care. Education for traditional birth attendants, community health workers, and parents is essential, as this condition is often linked to sexually transmitted infections.
